words.situation: You arrive at your partner's family home and the door opens. Greet them.
words.notes: The everyday greeting in Pakistan, for anyone, at any time of day. The person arriving says it first, and younger people greet elders first. Between friends it is often shortened to `salaam`.

hindi_variant.note: The usual greeting in Hindi films and TV. Muslim characters in films usually say `aadaab` or `salaam`; in Pakistan it's `assalaam-o-alaikum`.

words.meaning_en: hello (the reply: and peace be upon you)
words.situation: Someone greets you with assalaam-o-alaikum. Reply.

example.ur: وعلیکم السلام! ٹھیک ہوں، اور آپ؟
example.en: And peace be upon you! I'm fine, and you?

words.notes: Only ever a reply to `assalaam-o-alaikum`. Never say it first.
Goes with `huuN`: `maiN Thiik huuN` is "I'm fine". The same Urdu spelling میں also means "in" (`meN`); you'll meet that in Unit 4.
Never changes, whether you mean a man, a woman or a thing. On its own, `Thiik hai` means "OK" or "fine, agreed".
The respectful "you": for elders, in-laws, guests and anyone you don't know well. It always takes `haiN`, even for one person. Lesson 2 covers the two other words for "you".

words.situation: Your partner's father sits down next to you. Ask him politely how he is.

example.en: And peace be upon you! How are you?

words.notes: Asking a woman, say `aap kaisii haiN?`. The ending changes for a woman; Unit 2 shows the pattern behind it.

words.meaning_en: how are you? how are things?
words.situation: Your cousin rings for a chat. Ask how things are, in a relaxed way.
words.notes: Friendly, and the same whether you ask a man or a woman. Common answers are `Thiik hai` ("it's fine") or `maiN Thiik huuN`. To an elder you don't know well, `aap kaise haiN?` is more respectful.

words.situation: Someone asks how you are. Before saying you're well, give thanks to God, as most Pakistanis do.
words.notes: An Arabic phrase used by Muslims and heard constantly in Pakistani conversation, above all in answers to "how are you?". It can go before or after the rest: `alhamdulillaah, Thiik huuN` or `Thiik huuN, alhamdulillaah`.
`aur aap?` ("and you?") is the quickest way to return a question.
Comes straight after the word it adds to: `maiN bhii` is "me too", "I also".
The everyday "you" for friends, younger cousins and siblings, and children. It takes `ho`: `tum Thiik ho?` For elders and anyone you don't know well, use `aap`.

example.en: Are you all right, sweetheart? (a grandmother to a small child)

words.notes: The closest, most intimate "you": parents and grandparents to small children, very close friends, and God in prayers. You'll hear it all the time in songs. Said to an adult who isn't close, it's rude, so you'll mostly need to understand it rather than say it. It takes `hai`: `tuu Thiik hai?`

words.meaning_en: yes (politely); a word that adds respect
words.notes: On its own, `jii?` is the polite way to answer when someone calls you: "yes?". At the start of an answer it makes the whole answer respectful. It also follows family titles, as in `ammii jii` (Mum).

words.situation: Your partner's cousin, a man about your age, says hi. Ask him how he is, the friendly way.
words.notes: For friends, younger relatives and children. Asking a woman or a girl, say `tum kaisii ho?`.
Older relatives call anyone younger `beTaa` as a term of affection, girls as well as boys, grown-ups as well as children. Expect to hear it from your partner's parents.

words.meaning_en: daughter; (to a girl or young woman) dear

example.en: Are you all right, dear? (to a girl)

words.notes: Like `beTaa`, used affectionately by elders, here only for girls and women. Many elders just say `beTaa` to everyone.

words.meaning_en: child (a boy, or a child in general)
words.notes: The plural `bacche` means "children" or "the kids", and is a very common question to parents: `bacche Thiik haiN?` A girl is `bacchii`.
Masculine for a male friend, feminine for a female friend. The plural doesn't change: one `dost`, two `dost`. Friends call each other `tum`.
Present forms: `maiN huuN`, `tuu hai`, `tum ho`, `aap haiN`, `ham haiN`; one person or thing `hai`, several `haiN`. They go at the end of the sentence.
Takes `haiN`: `ham Thiik haiN`. In Hindi films you'll sometimes hear `ham` used to mean "I"; in everyday Pakistani Urdu it means "we".
A masculine noun that ends in `-ii`. The plural doesn't change: one `paRosii`, two `paRosii`. A woman next door is often called `paRosan`, but `paRosii` is fine for anyone, and for a mixed group.
The English word, used by everyone. Urdu has no word for "a": `maiN doctor huuN` is "I'm a doctor". A GP is often addressed as `doctor saahab`.
In the UK, people just use the English word. Like other English nouns, it doesn't take an English -s in the plural: `ham student haiN`.

words.meaning_en: Mr; sir (after a name or a job, for respect)
words.notes: Goes after a man's name or job to show respect: `imraan saahab`, `doctor saahab`. Talking about someone you call `saahab`, use `haiN`, even for one person. For women, people usually use a family title instead; you'll meet these in Unit 3.
Usually near the start of the sentence: `aaj maiN Thiik huuN` or `maiN aaj Thiik huuN`.

example.ur: اب میں ٹھیک ہوں، الحمد للہ۔

words.notes: Handy after an illness or a bad day: `ab Thiik huuN` ("I'm fine now").

words.meaning_en: this; he, she, it (someone or something near you)
words.notes: Points to someone or something close by. It doesn't say whether it's a man or a woman: `ye Thiik hai` is "he's fine" or "she's fine". Spelt یہ but said `ye`.

words.meaning_en: that; he, she, it (someone or something further away)
words.notes: For someone further away or not here at all. Like `ye`, it doesn't say whether it's a man or a woman. Spelt وہ but said `wo`.
Matches the person you're talking about, not you: `meraa bhaaii`, `merii behen`. With an elder you respect, `meraa` becomes `mere`: `mere abbuu`. Unit 3 explains the pattern.
The usual word for Mum in Pakistani families, often with `jii`: `ammii jii`. Always with the respectful `haiN`. Many British Pakistani families also say `mummy`.

hindi_variant.note: What you'll mostly hear in Hindi films and songs. Urdu speakers use `maaN` too, in poetry and emotional moments.

words.notes: The usual word for Dad, often with `jii`: `abbuu jii`. Always with the respectful plural: `mere abbuu haiN`, not `meraa abbuu hai`. Some families say `abbaa` or `papa`.

hindi_variant.note: The respectful "father" in Hindi films; younger characters often just say `papa`.

words.notes: A masculine noun ending in `-ii`; the plural doesn't change. Also a friendly way to address any man about your age or a bit older, even a shopkeeper: `bilaal bhaaii`.
Spelt بہن but said `behen`. The plural is `behneN` (sisters). A younger sister usually gets `hai`; an older one often gets the respectful `haiN`.
Introduced with respect, as `mere shauhar haiN`. In relaxed speech many women say `miyaaN` instead.

hindi_variant.note: The usual word in Hindi films and TV.

words.notes: Introducing your wife to elders, the respectful `haiN` is polite; among friends `merii biiwii hai` is normal too. `merii` stays the same either way.

hindi_variant.note: The usual word in Hindi films and TV.

words.notes: On its own it's casual, for friends and family your age. With elders and strangers, say `jii haaN` or just `jii`.
As "not", it goes straight before the verb at the end: `wo Thiik nahiiN hai`. The verb is often dropped after it: `maiN doctor nahiiN` is just as normal. People type it `nahi`, `nai` or `nhi`.

words.situation: Your partner's father asks if you're well. Say yes, politely.
words.notes: The safe "yes" with anyone older or anyone you don't know well. Plain `jii` means the same.

words.situation: The receptionist at your GP surgery asks if you're a doctor. You aren't. Say no, politely.
words.notes: A plain `nahiiN` to an elder can sound abrupt; `jii nahiiN` softens it.

words.meaning_en: what?; (at the start) makes a yes/no question
words.notes: At the start of a sentence, `kyaa` just marks a yes/no question, like "do" or "is" in English; nothing else moves. Elsewhere it means "what", as in `kyaa haal hai?`.

words.situation: A neighbour asks you something and you have no idea. Say so.
words.notes: The everyday "dunno". To an elder, `jii, pataa nahiiN` sounds softer. Often typed `pata nahi` or `pta nhi`.
A warm, keen "yes": `jii, zaruur!` is the perfect answer to an invitation.
Usually at the start of the sentence. On its own, `shaayad` is "maybe", and `shaayad nahiiN` is "maybe not".
Never changes, like `Thiik`: a man, a woman and a group are all `tayyaar`. Also written `taiyaar`; typing either is fine.
